build_hon(): higher-order networks from sequences

honets

2026-08-26

The analytic question

A transition network answers “what follows what”. It cannot answer “what follows what, given how you got here” — because a first-order node is just a state, with no memory of the path that reached it.

build_hon() builds a network whose nodes carry that memory. A node like Specify -> Command is the state Command together with the fact that Specify preceded it, and it keeps its own continuation distribution. The network only creates such a node when the evidence justifies it: the BuildHON+ rule of Xu, Wickramarathne & Chawla (2016) adds a higher-order context only if its continuation distribution differs meaningfully from the lower-order one it would otherwise inherit.

library(honets)
library(cograph)

The data are human_long: 10,796 coded human turns from 429 human-AI pair-programming sessions, nine action codes.

Building one

Long-format event data goes in directly — name the action, actor and time columns and build_hon() does the splitting.

hon <- build_hon(human_long,
                 action = "code", actor = "session_id", time = "timestamp",
                 max_order = 3, min_freq = 5)
hon
Higher-Order Network (HON)
  Nodes:        233 (9 first-order states)
  Edges:        819
  Max order:    3 (requested 3)
  Min freq:     5
  Trajectories: 425

Nine states, but 233 nodes. The extra 224 are memory contexts that earned their place. max_order = 3 is a ceiling, not a target: the rule extraction stops promoting a context as soon as the higher order stops paying.

summary() adds the order breakdown:

summary(hon)
Higher-Order Network (HON) Summary
  Nodes: 233 | Edges: 819 | Trajectories: 425
  First-order states: Command, Correct, Frustrate, Inquire, Interrupt, Refine, Request, Specify, Verify
  Max order observed: 3 (requested: 3)
  Min frequency: 5
  Node order distribution:
    Order 1: 9 nodes
    Order 2: 74 nodes
    Order 3: 150 nodes

Reading the rules

as.data.frame() is the accessor. Each row is one extracted rule: a source context, a target state, how often it occurred, and the conditional probability.

as.data.frame(hon, sort_by = "count", top = 6)
                  path    from        to count probability from_order to_order
1   Specify -> Command Specify   Command   740   0.2640971          1        2
2   Request -> Specify Request   Specify   630   0.6158358          1        2
3   Command -> Specify Command   Specify   549   0.2767137          1        2
4   Specify -> Specify Specify   Specify   481   0.1716631          1        2
5   Command -> Command Command   Command   475   0.2394153          1        2
6 Specify -> Interrupt Specify Interrupt   466   0.1663098          1        2

Read the first row as: of all the times Specify was followed by something, 26.4% of the time it was Command — 740 occurrences. That one is first-order (from_order = 1), which is the baseline the higher-order rules have to beat.

The genuinely higher-order rules are the ones with from_order >= 2:

as.data.frame(hon, order_min = 2, sort_by = "count", top = 6)
                                      path                          from
1            Specify -> Command -> Specify            Specify -> Command
2            Command -> Request -> Specify            Command -> Request
3            Specify -> Command -> Request            Specify -> Command
4          Request -> Specify -> Interrupt            Request -> Specify
5 Specify -> Command -> Request -> Specify Specify -> Command -> Request
6            Command -> Command -> Command            Command -> Command
         to count probability from_order to_order
1   Specify   284   0.3901099          2        2
2   Specify   231   0.7674419          2        3
3   Request   199   0.2733516          2        3
4 Interrupt   189   0.3258621          2        2
5   Specify   181   0.9679144          3        3
6   Command   177   0.3881579          2        2

Seeing it

Do not draw the higher-order network itself. It has 233 nodes, one per memory context, and splot() on it is an unreadable hairball. The network you draw is the first-order one — nine states — and the higher-order structure goes on top of it as pathways.

net1 <- build_hon(human_long, action = "code", actor = "session_id",
                  time = "timestamp", max_order = 1, min_freq = 5)
c(nodes = net1$n_nodes, edges = net1$n_edges)
nodes edges 
    9    81

net_hon is dual-classed cograph_network, so cograph draws it with no conversion step.

splot(net1, minimum = 0.05,
      title = "Human actions in AI-assisted coding")

plot_simplicial() puts the extracted rules on that same nine-node layout: each blob is one context and the state it predicts, sources in blue and the target in red. Repeated states get distinct positions, so Command -> Command -> Correct covers three visible nodes rather than collapsing onto one. Pass the rules through pathways = — this is the same table as.data.frame() returns, read as shape rather than as rows.

plot_simplicial(net1,
                pathways = as.data.frame(hon, order_min = 2,
                                         sort_by = "count", top = 6),
                max_pathways = 6,
                title = "Six strongest extracted rules")

How much of the network is higher-order?

table(as.data.frame(hon)$from_order)

  1   2   3 
 81 441 297

81 first-order rules — the full 9×9 transition structure, since on data this dense every pair occurs. Then 441 second-order and 297 third-order rules were added on top. Roughly nine in ten rules in this network encode memory.

min_freq is the consequential choice

A context is only considered if it occurs at least min_freq times. This is the main lever on network size, and it is a statement about how much evidence you require before believing a memory effect.

sizes <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(5, 20, 50, 100), function(mf) {
  h <- build_hon(human_long, action = "code", actor = "session_id",
                 time = "timestamp", max_order = 3, min_freq = mf)
  data.frame(min_freq = mf, nodes = h$n_nodes, edges = h$n_edges,
             max_order_observed = h$max_order_observed)
}))
sizes
  min_freq nodes edges max_order_observed
1        5   233   819                  3
2       20    72   223                  3
3       50    23    85                  3
4      100    15    37                  3

The network shrinks from 233 nodes to 15 as the evidence bar rises. All four still observe order-3 contexts — the strongest memory effects survive even a demanding threshold, which is reassuring. Report the threshold with any result: a claim about a 233-node network and a claim about a 15-node network are different claims.

Accepted input

build_hon() takes sequences in whichever shape you have them.

# a list of character vectors
build_hon(list(c("A", "B", "C", "A", "B"), c("B", "C", "A", "B")),
          max_order = 2, min_freq = 1)
Higher-Order Network (HON)
  Nodes:        3 (3 first-order states)
  Edges:        3
  Max order:    1 (requested 2)
  Min freq:     1
  Trajectories: 2
# a wide data.frame, one sequence per row, trailing NAs stripped
build_hon(data.frame(V1 = c("A", "B"), V2 = c("B", "C"), V3 = c("C", NA)),
          max_order = 2, min_freq = 1)
Higher-Order Network (HON)
  Nodes:        3 (3 first-order states)
  Edges:        2
  Max order:    1 (requested 2)
  Min freq:     1
  Trajectories: 2

It also accepts a fitted tna or netobject model directly, decoding integer-coded states back to their labels.

What to do next

  • markov_order_test() — the prior question. Is there memory in these sequences at all? Run it before reporting a higher-order network as evidence of anything.
  • path_dependence() — which contexts carry the memory, one row per context, with the divergence that justifies it.
  • bootstrap_hon() — do these rules survive resampling? A rule extracted once is not yet a finding.
  • hon_centrality() — rank the states using the higher-order topology.
  • build_honem() — embed the nodes in a vector space.
  • build_simplicial(type = "pathway") — read the same fitted network as a simplicial complex.

References

  • Xu, J., Wickramarathne, T. L., & Chawla, N. V. (2016). Representing higher-order dependencies in networks. Science Advances, 2(5), e1600028.
  • Saebi, M., Xu, J., Kaplan, L. M., Ribeiro, B., & Chawla, N. V. (2020). Efficient modeling of higher-order dependencies in networks: from algorithm to application for anomaly detection. EPJ Data Science, 9, 15.
